opus-5.5.text:
I think it came mostly from experience rather than from some grand plan. Early on, when I was a student, I was quite drawn to the elegant side of machine learning: new models, nice formulations, clever optimization tricks. That was exciting, and I learned a lot from it. But over time I noticed that the work I felt most proud of, and the work that ended up mattering to other people, almost always started from a concrete pain point rather than from a method looking for an application.

A good example is the boosted trees work that became XGBoost. The starting point wasn't "let me invent a new algorithm." It was more like, people are trying to solve real prediction problems, the existing tools are too slow, they don't scale, they're awkward to use, so what would it take to make this actually work well? Once you start from that question, you end up touching everything: the algorithm, the systems side, memory layout, distributed computing, even the user interface. And you discover that a lot of the interesting research questions are hiding in those details.

The same thing happened later with deep learning systems and compilers, like TVM. The problem was very tangible: we have all these models and all these different hardware backends, and it takes enormous human effort to make each combination fast. That problem pulled us into compilers, into learning-based optimization, into hardware. I wouldn't have predicted that path if I'd started from a fixed methodology.

So the preference grew out of that pattern. When you're problem-first, you're not attached to a particular hammer. You're willing to cross boundaries between machine learning, systems, and hardware, because the problem doesn't care about those boundaries. And I think that's where a lot of the real opportunities are, in the gaps between fields.

Another part of it is feedback. When you build something that people actually use, you get very direct signals: what's broken, what's slow, what's confusing. That keeps you honest, and it often points you to the next research question. Open source has been really important for me in that sense. The community tells you what the real problems are.

That doesn't mean I think method-driven research isn't valuable. It absolutely is, and many big breakthroughs come from people pushing an idea deeply. But for me personally, starting from a real problem gives me motivation, and it makes it more likely that the work ends up having an impact beyond the paper.

r001.rationale: Contrasts methods seeking applications with starting from concrete problems, and says this approach avoids attachment to a particular “hammer.”

r002.rationale: Says solving a real problem provides personal motivation and describes building useful tools while remaining willing to cross fields rather than stick to one method.

r003.rationale: Does not propose testing whether non-neural-network models could match ImageNet-like results at massive scale.

r004.rationale: Describes existing tools for prediction as too slow and unscalable, then says the tree work led into algorithm and systems concerns, including distributed computing.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly it wasn't something I set out to have as a philosophy. It kind of grew out of the work.

When I was doing my undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, I was in the ACM class, and a lot of what we did was very competition-driven. You get a problem, you solve it, you move on. That trains a certain mindset, but it's also a bit artificial, because someone else has decided the problem is worth solving. Later, when I started working on things like XGBoost, the motivation was really concrete. I was competing in Kaggle challenges, and I needed a gradient boosting implementation that was fast enough and flexible enough to actually iterate with. The tools at the time weren't cutting it. So I built one. I didn't think of it as a research contribution at first. It was just a thing I needed.

And then watching how people picked it up taught me something. The parts people cared about weren't always the parts I thought were clever. They cared that it ran on their data, that it didn't crash, that it fit into their workflow. That shifted how I think. A good problem is one where, if you solve it, something real changes for somebody. If you start from a technique and go looking for a place to apply it, you often end up with results that look nice on paper but nobody uses.

The same pattern repeated with MXNet and later TVM. With TVM, the problem was very clear: we had all these models and all these different hardware backends, and the engineering effort to make each pair work well was enormous. Nobody wanted to hand-write kernels for every new chip. So the question became, can we build a compiler stack that automates a lot of that. The research questions came out of that need, not the other way around.

I'd also say there's a practical reason I lean this way. When you start from a real problem, you get constant feedback. Users complain, benchmarks don't move, something breaks on a new GPU. That feedback keeps you honest. Pure technique-driven research can drift for a long time without anyone telling you it's going in the wrong direction.

So I guess the short version is: I developed it by building things people actually used, and paying attention to what they did with them. That ended up being a better teacher than any abstract idea about what research should look like.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts technique-driven research with starting from a real problem, but does not say the problem class can be addressed with different methods.

r002.rationale: It says building useful things shaped Chen’s approach, but does not connect that motivation to reluctance to restrict his research to a particular method.

r003.rationale: It does not propose testing whether non-neural-network models could achieve ImageNet-like success at massive scale.

r004.rationale: It describes needing a faster, more flexible gradient-boosting implementation, but does not explain that tree-model computational bottlenecks led Chen into machine-learning systems research.

astra-6.text:
For me, it’s about starting with something concrete: what are we trying to do, and what is preventing us from doing it? In machine learning, it’s very easy to become excited about a particular technique and then look for places to apply it. I find it more useful to go in the other direction—to understand the problem first, and then ask what tools we need.

That preference develops through the process of building things. You start with an idea, try to make it work, and discover that the actual bottleneck may be different from what you expected. That feedback helps you refine the research question. Sometimes the answer needs a new method; sometimes it needs a better system; sometimes it needs something much simpler.

So I think of problem-first research as staying open about the solution while being very clear about what you want to enable. The exciting part is when solving a concrete problem reveals a more general question.

r001.rationale: It contrasts pursuing a favored technique with starting from a concrete problem and choosing among methods, systems, or simpler tools to solve it.

r002.rationale: It links building things to developing this preference and says to stay open about the solution, conveying a motivation to create without being tied to one method.

r003.rationale: It does not propose testing whether non-neural-network models could match ImageNet-like success at massive scale.

r004.rationale: It mentions discovering bottlenecks and sometimes needing a better system, but does not connect tree-model computational limits to entering machine-learning systems research.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, that preference developed through the experience of building things. You start with an idea that looks interesting, but when you try to make it work in a real system, you discover that the important problem is sometimes different from the one you originally imagined.

That feedback is really valuable. It pushes me to ask: What are we trying to enable? What is preventing us from doing that today? Once that is clear, we can choose the techniques that help, and sometimes develop new ones.

I still think curiosity about methods is important. But I like having a concrete problem as an anchor, because it gives you a way to judge whether you are making progress. And often, if you understand a particular problem deeply enough, you find ideas that are useful much more broadly.

r001.rationale: The response says to choose techniques that help solve a concrete problem, but does not clearly contrast favored-method research with solving a class of problems using different methods.

r002.rationale: It links Chen’s preference to building things, but does not connect that motivation to reluctance to restrict his research to a particular method.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention testing non-neural-network models against ImageNet-like success at massive scale.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention tree models, computational bottlenecks, or a move into machine-learning systems research.
